<reason>Side B (PRO) won a high-quality exchange. CON built a genuinely strong case around the enforcement ladder (fines are a price, not a relocation), secondary movement, and the strategic claim that PRO's fallback "dissolves" into a capacity fund. But PRO answered each pressure directly: "Hungary is not Europe" (a rule binding 23 states with 4 buy-outs still transforms who carries the load), matched allocation as the cure for absconding ("CON cannot simultaneously argue people flee assignments and object when the assignment goes where they were headed"), and — decisively in the closing — the perform-or-pay reframe: a quota with a buy-out is an obligation with two discharge routes, and the quota is what turns money from charity into debt ("Under the status quo, Greece asks. Under this motion, Greece is owed"). CON's throughput reframe also sat awkwardly against the motion as written, since its own alternative leaves frontline states managing most arrivals — the exact arrangement the proposition rejects — and PRO exploited this with "Lesbos as Europe's permanent processing warehouse, subsidised." Both sides used plausible background knowledge without fake precision; both answered pressure questions in proper A1/A2 format. PRO's arguments tracked the motion more faithfully and its closing crystallized the live clash more cleanly, giving it a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pivotal sequence was CON's Q1 ("what physically happens on the ladder's last rung?") met by PRO's A1 ("the money moves and the caseload moves with it... a rule that binds twenty-three states and is bought out by four is still a transformation"), and then CON's "dissolution trap" in Rebuttal 2/Closing met by PRO's perform-or-pay answer: delete the quota and the money is charity; keep it and the money is a debt. That final exchange neutralized CON's strongest strategic move and decided the debate.</best_rebuttal>
